library(readr); library(here)
fail_n <- tryCatch(length(yaml::read_yaml(here("tests","expected_failures.yaml"))$expected_failures), error = function(e) NA)
skip_n <- tryCatch(length(yaml::read_yaml(here("tests","expected_skips.yaml"))$expected_skips), error = function(e) NA)

## Abstract

Reproducible-research practice has converged on a good answer to *can this
analysis be re-run*: version control, a pinned environment, a declarative
pipeline, continuous integration. It has no comparable answer to a different
question: *which parts of this analysis are not settled, and who is supposed to
settle them.* In a retrospective cohort study of conference abstracts we found
that the second question dominated. Most of what threatened the results was not
code that failed but code that succeeded while resting on a decision nobody had
made, or on a measurement nobody had validated. We describe a governance layer
built to make those two failure modes visible: an expected-failure manifest that
registers open scientific decisions as deliberately failing tests, an estimand
fingerprint that fails when the target quantity changes silently, a row-level
data contract, and a claims registry binding every number in the manuscript to
the file that produces it. We report what it caught.

## The problem

A continuous-integration suite answers a binary question: did the code do what
the tests say. That is necessary and it is not the hard part of an observational
study. The hard parts look like this:

* A covariate is derived by a rule nobody has validated, and the rule is wrong
  about half the time.
* A parser silently drops two thirds of its input and writes the failure to disk
  as data, so every downstream completeness check reports success.
* An outcome is decided by the order of four branches in a `case_when()`, and
  that order encodes a scientific position no author has taken.
* A denominator changes and every reported number moves with it, correctly, so
  nothing fails.

None of these is a bug in the sense CI understands. Each is a question that code
cannot answer, sitting in a place where code will answer it anyway, by default,
invisibly.

## The governance layer

**Expected-failure manifest.** Tests that encode open questions are written to
fail and registered in `tests/expected_failures.yaml` with a reason and the
decision they wait on. The suite gate treats the manifest as the definition of
green: it fails on any unregistered failure, and equally when a registered test
starts passing, when an entry names a test that no longer runs, or when a test
skips without approval. The rules are declared as data in `config/ci_contract.yml`
so the gate and the workflows cannot disagree.

The second rule is the one that matters. A list of known-failing tests rots: a
decision is taken, the entry stays, and CI keeps green-lighting a settled
question. Failing when an entry starts passing forces the registry to shrink as
decisions are made.

**Estimand fingerprint.** The parameters that define the target quantity -
population, denominator rule, outcome definition, time origin, censoring - are
recorded in a baseline. A drift report rebuilds the fingerprint and fails when it
differs. Changing the estimand then requires an explicit act with a commit
message, rather than being a side effect of editing configuration. This is
distinct from checking that values are right: an analysis can produce a perfectly
reconcilable number for a question nobody intended to ask.

**Row-level data contract.** Aggregate checks hide row-level corruption. A
dataset can carry the right row count, the right rate and the right median while
individual rows contradict themselves. The contract declares per-column and
cross-field invariants and reports the offending identifier. It is implemented
with pointblank.

**Claims registry.** Every quantitative claim in the manuscript is a row carrying
its value, the file it comes from, an expression that recovers it, a tolerance
and where it appears. A test recomputes each one. Prose that quotes a number no
file produces any more fails the suite.

**Mutation testing of the guards.** Half of the data-contract tests corrupt a
copy of the data and require the checker to catch it. Zero violations is only
meaningful if the validator can find one; a broken validator is indistinguishable
from a healthy dataset.

## What it caught

`r fail_n` decisions are currently registered as open. The following were found
by the layer itself rather than by review.

**A parser that disguised its own failure.** An affiliation extractor located
author affiliations correctly and discarded them, because one of two regular
expressions had been updated for a change in the source format and the other had
not. Unresolved values reached a `paste()` and were written to disk as the string
`"NA | NA"`. The column therefore looked populated: 1,874 rows held NA-token
strings that no missingness check could see, and a model input sat at zero of
1,106 populated for months without anything noticing. 661 of 1,154 source files
were affected. It surfaced only when a covariate audit asked why one variable had
no evidence for two of twelve congress years.

**A covariate measuring the wrong construct.** The same audit showed that
`is_academic`, described as institutional affiliation, was derived from abstract
body text using patterns including "residency" and "fellowship" - words that
describe a study, not an author's institution. Against real affiliations it
agreed 54% of the time and understated academic affiliation by half. A companion
variable, US-based status, overstated its prevalence by 24 percentage points.
Bootstrap retention had been falling for three refits; the audit explained why.

**An outcome decided by branch order.** Whether an abstract counted as published
depended on the order of branches in a single `case_when()`. Two positions
nobody had argued for were encoded there: that a publication predating the
congress could still count as a conversion if a reviewer confirmed the paper, and
that a `definite` score outranked a human reviewer's rejection. Registering both
as failing tests forced them to be decided. Both were reversed.

**A guard that caught a schema change.** Implementing one of those decisions
required joining a reviewer column into the cascade. Left in place it widened the
analytical dataset by one column and tripped the documentation-drift test - a
rule change should not silently reshape the dataset.

## What it costs

The layer is roughly 2,000 lines of tests and configuration against a 6,000-line
analysis. It is not free, and two costs are worth naming.

It slows changes that ought to be fast, because a covariate redefinition now
requires updating the claims registry, the estimand baseline and the prose
together. That is the intended trade, but it is a trade.

And it can encourage registering a decision rather than taking it. The
manifest ceiling exists for this reason: the registry is meant to shrink, and
growing it past a stated limit must be deliberate.

## What it does not do

It does not detect a wrong-but-plausible number. Every check here is either an
identity, a contract, or a comparison against a recorded baseline. An analysis
that is internally consistent, reconciles with its own outputs and targets its
declared estimand can still be wrong about the world. The affiliation parser was
caught by a human asking why a variable behaved oddly, not by a test.

The layer's claim is narrower: it makes the unsettled parts of an analysis
visible and keeps them visible until someone settles them.

## Availability

Code, data and the full decision registry are at
https://github.com/mufflyt/abstract_lifetime. The registry generated from the
manifest is `docs/DECISIONS_PENDING.md`; the governance mechanics are
`docs/TEST_GOVERNANCE.md`.
